speechtext:
Mr. H. E. BRUNELLE (Champlain) moved the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Lord's Day Act.
He said: Supported as I am by La Ligue du Dimanche, by the great majority of the citizens of the province of Quebec, by countless societies and labour unions, and also by the Lord's Day Alliance, I feel it my duty to bring again before this house an amendment to the Lord's Day Act similar to the one which was adopted by the house last year. It will be remembered that my bill of last year purported solely to increase the penalties under the Lord's Day Act in order, to use a common expression, to give teeth to that law.
The reasons for the amendment I moved last year still hold good, and it is not my intention to repeat them to-night.
It was in the senate that the bill received its death-blow. When it came back from that body there was nothing left of its original tenor; it was changed from beginning to end. The senate pretended to have adequately amended the Lord's Day Act by increasing the maximum fines and leaving the minimum fines practically as they were before.. But, as all corporations have the means to prepare the strongest legal defences, it follows that nothing but minimum fines would, in most instances, be imposed and the violation of the law would continue. It was inconsistent for those in the other place to say that no corporations were violating the law, and at the same time to pretend to impose more severe sanctions. On the other hand, if there is, as is alleged, no violation of the Lord's Day Act, why should there be any fear of stricter sanctions?
My bill purports solely to give bo our courts the discretionary power to impose gaol sentences upon those who make their employees work on Sundays. Let me read the amendment :
Section 14 of the Lord's Day Act. chapter 123 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. 1927, is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
(2) Any person, being a director, an officer, a superintendent or an employee of a corporation, to whose direction or orders any employee is by tire terms or conditions of his employment bound to conform, who authorizes or directs any such last mentioned employee of that corporation to carry on any part of the business of the corporation in violation of any of the provisions of this act. shall be liable, on summary conviction before two justices of the peace, to similar penalties to those to which a corporation is liable under subsection 1 of this section, or for a first offence, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months and not less than one month, with or without hard labour, and for each subsequent offence, to impi'isonment for a term not exceeding six months and not less than two months, with or without hard labour.
An amendment which only increases the minimum fine is, in my opinion, a fool-trap. In fact, the hon. senator for Parkdale made the following statement as to last year's amendment by the senate:
I regard the amendment as merely a wooden gun with which to do some hunting. I think it is absolutely useless for the purpose of accomplishing what all hon. members of the committee desire, that is. to prevent unnecessary work on Sunday, which has prevailed in certain parts of the country.
He continued:
It seems to me that every time an important measure comes up here which contemplates the protection of the less fortunate members
Lord's Day Act-Violation

of Canada's society we devote our entire attention to the question whether we may not be doing an injustice to somebody higher up in the Canadian social scale. Personally, I think it is wrong. I think this provision is entirely useless, and simply amounts to the hunting of violators of the Lord's Day Act with a wooden gun.
Since the only objections came from the other chamber last year, it is my duty to confine my remarks to those objections. Imaginary fears and impossible dangers of all sorts were alleged as arguments against the bill which I introduced last year and which I reintroduce now. Let me refute those arguments by stating that we all know and admit that some works or operations of continuous process can be done on Sunday. Some one brought out as an objection to my bill that certain operations of continuous process compelled some plants to operate on Sunday, and concluded that, if my amendment were passed, the directors of those particular corporations or plants would be liable to imprisonment.
Before raising such a futile and frivolous objection, one should take pains to read the law as it now stands. The Lord's Day Act permits the following work to be done on Sunday. Section 11. paragraph (d), provides:
Starting or maintaining fires, making repairs to furnaces, and repairs in cases of emergency, and doing any other work when such fires, repairs, or work are essential to any industry or industrial process of such a continuous nature that it cannot be stopped without serious injury to such industry, or its product or to the plant or property used in such process.
My amendment does not restrict this exception. Some one else objected to my amendment because certain industries, such as the canning industiy, must occasionally operate on Sunday, and said that my bill would render the directors of such industries liable to imprisonment for having done nothing but urgent work. Perhaps that objector should in the first place have read paragraphs (e), (m) and (w) of section 11 of the Lord's Day Act, which permit the following works on Sunday. Paragraph (m) refers to perishable products which would apply to the canning industry, and it reads:
(m) The caring for milk, cheese, and live animals and the unloading of and caring for perishable products and live animals, arriving at any point during the Lord's day.
Paragraph (w) reads:
(w) Any unavoidable work on the Lord's day to save property in cases of emergency, or where such property is in imminent danger of destruction or serious injury.
[Mr. Brunelle.l
And paragraph (e) reads:
(e) Starting or maintaining fires, and ventilating, hunting out and inspecting mines, when any such work is essential to the protection of property, life or health.
These exceptions do not cover the whole ground; section 11 itself makes provision for others. Section Id reads:
Notwithstanding anything herein contained, any person may on the Lord's day do any work of necessity or mercy, and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the ordinary meaning of the expression "work of necessity or mercy," it is hereby declared, that it shall be deemed to include the following classes of work.
There are exceptions particularly mentioned, but there may be others according to the circumstances of each case. On the other hand, ample protection to all is accorded from other sources.
In the first place, the provision for imprisonment mentioned in my bill is only an alternative; the courts would be free to impose the same penalties as before if they thought fit. In the second place, the attorney general for each province cannot fail to look into the circumstances of each case before a prosecution is started. We all know that instructions to prosecute for violations of the Lord's Day Act must come from the attorney general of the province in which the offence occurs. I refer to section 16 of the act:
No action or prosecution for a violation of this act shall be commenced without the leave of the attorney general for the province in which the offence is alleged to have been committed, nor after the expiration of sixty days from the time of the commission of the alleged offence.
In the third place, our courts are fair and equitable, and they would always take into consideration whatever extenuating circumstances might be alleged in favour of those who find it urgent and necessary to work on Sunday.
In reality, if my amendment were accepted, directors or officers of corporations need do only one simple thing to protect themselves; let them definitely and officially notify their superintendents or managers not to do on Sunday any work which is forbidden by the Lord's Day Act, and then there would be no more violations of the law. If there be violations, I submit that directors or officers of corporations, who often are away from the scene of operation of their plants, having given this notice, would have a good defence to any action started against them. Undoubtedly some plants operate on Sunday in violation of the act. Again and again I have seen workmen passing in front of my house on Sundays 'with their lunch boxes, on their

Lord's Day Act-Violation
way to the mill to do some work which I know is not urgent. Some transport companies send their trucks out to work on Sundays in violation of the Lord's Day Act, and I am sure some stores and places of business do business on Sunday in violation of the provisions of that act.
I am not a fanatic; I am not moved by excessive religious zeal. Some provincial authorities have the monopoly of such extravagant virtues; I do not want to be a competitor with them in that field. I do not want to do harm to the directors or officers of our corporations, to those who may be innocent or who violate the law in good faith. What I do want is that the penalties under the Lord's Day Act should reach those particular directors or officers who, through indifference or lack of respect for the Christian views of their workmen, do not hesitate to set them to work on Sunday. That is all I want. My humble opinion is that the penalties at present set forth in the Lord's Day Act are not a sufficient deterrent.
The amendment which was made to my bill of last year created an injustice. These corporation plants are built and run with money subscribed by shareholders and bondholders, and it is wrong that directors or officers who allow the law to be violated, should, instead of being personally liable to the penalty, make the funds of the corporation liable. Those funds belong to the bondholders or shareholders, who are not responsible for violations of the law. Those who are responsible should be personally punished.
It is not my intention to say any more, because this bill is identical with that unanimously adopted by this house last year.

The reasons why I seconded this motion are, first, that violation of the Lord's Day Act is a breaking of the moral law; second that it is breaking the law of fair play; and third, that it is breaking the law of the land. The moral law is, "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." The Right Hon. Ramsey MacDonald said that a nation that respects one day in seven to rest from toil and worship the Almighty will find this a great bulwark in the upbuilding of manhood in that nation. We cannot break the moral law and not suffer for it; as someone has said, "If we break the moral law, the moral law will break us."
There is in the act a safeguard permitting works of necessity and mercy. But, like my hon. friend, I know of very many instances where men have had to do on Sunday work which was neither necessary nor a work of mercy, but a work of graft. I should not say graft, but it was work in which the toiler was not considered in any way.
Another reason why I support this bill is that if more men were employed there would be less need for Sunday work, and therefore it would be in a small way a cure for unemployment. When we see men carrying their dinner pails and going to work on Sunday while they see other people released from their toil and going to places of worship where they receive some inspiration, encouragement and instruction, it tends to create a sense of defeat in them, and it is not fair. Those of us who were brought up in homes where we were taught to do our daily toil in six days of the week and to be ready on Sunday for rest and worship, feel that working seven days a week is not fair play.
The hon. member says he is not a fanatic with set views on religion. I have some set views. One such view is that there must be a definite standard, and that standard is the Master Workman of Galilee. When we were engaged on construction work, the plumb-line was the standard; if the building did not conform to that plumb-line, it had to be pulled down and built straight. When we test our conduct by (he example of the Master Workman of Galilee, then the Sabbath day will have its rightful place.

7. In connection with underground pumping and the maintenance of shafts and underground equipment, it is obvious that one or more hoisting engines would generally have to be operated intermittently on Sunday to raise or lower men or materials.
5.	Where crushing is done underground and where it is impracticable to store sufficient ore on surface to carry a mill or smelter over Sunday, it should be permissible, as an emergency measure, to hoist sufficient ore on Sundays to ensure the necessary continuous operation of mill or smelter, but every effort should be made to keep such work to a minimum.
9.	Shaft sinking operations should only be done on Sundays where bad ground or a heavy inflow of water makes it unsafe to interrupt such operations on Sundays.
I want to direct particular attention to the next paragraph:
10.	To prevent over-zealous subordinates from violating the spirit of the above code, we suggest that a copy or copies of this memorandum be kept posted in a conspicuous place at every mining property and that every department head or foreman be instructed to get special authorization from the manager or other person in charge before undertaking any work on Sunday other than the usual continuous operations mentioned above and routine repairs and maintenance.
They conclude with this:
While the association does not wish to presume to interpret any laws now existing, or which may hereafter be enacted, and can take no responsibility for the legal position of any members resulting from the observance of the

Lord's Day Act-Violation
above code, we believe that the above listed operations are works of necessity or mercy, and feel that if every effort is made to adhere to this code the mining industry can expect a friendly cooperation from the public and the authorities who are charged with the responsibility of ensuring the proper observation of Sunday.
That indicates the attitude of the mining men in the association towards Sunday labour in their industry. Notwithstanding that fact, and that they have clearly outlined to inspectors and others that such is their attitude, five charges have been laid against them for non-compliance with the act. Apparently the attorney general of the province, as is within his right, has approved the institution of these actions. To date, however, not one of them has come before the courts, so that the mining companies still have the axe suspended over their heads.
Corresponding recently with the association, I suggested that probably an amendment to the law should be made under the provisions of "works of necessity," so as more clearly to define such works as applied to the mining industry. The reply of the president to my suggestion is as follows:
There are a number of specific operations given in the Lord's Day Act as illustrations of what could be construed as "works of necessity and mercy," but I think it is generally understood that these specific operations were only given as illustrations and I don't see any point to increasing the number of illustrations, because it would be impossible to cover all operations that were necessary as "works of necessity and mercy" and if too many specific acts were mentioned, it might give the impression that it would be lawful to do only such specific operations as were specifically mentioned in the act.
That is the position in which the mining industry finds itself to-day under the act, whereby an over-zealous inspector, ignorant of his duties, may enter prosecutions against them.
As I said a little while ago, it is true that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Champlain has no bearing whatsoever upon that particular phase of the act. But it has the bearing that the companies feel to-day they are under suspicion of the authorities of our province. While to-day they are subject to a fine, if this amendment were to be accepted and became Law they would be liable to be thrown into prison, and to that feature they take decided exception.
May I place before the house a further paragraph from the communication I received from the president of the association, in which he gives his opinion as to what he believes would be fitting punishment under the law.
He suggests an increased fine, and his words are as follows:
The objection we have to Hr. Bruuelle's amendment is that while we expect and intend to obey both the letter and spirit of the law, from our recent experience we know that an inspector who does not know anything about mining and. therefore, what constitutes "work of necessity or mercy" at a mine, may come in and lay a charge and then a summons is served and . . . the mine manager may then be thrown into gaol because of a misunderstanding or difference of opinion as to the interpretation of the law. He might, of course, appeal and ultimately win his case, but in the meantime he would be subjected to the stigma of a lawbreaker and a criminal and we do not believe that it is necessary to do this in ordeT to ensure proper yespect for and observance of the Lord's Day Act. We contend that the present system of fines is sufficient to ensure proper observance of the act and if the fine is not sufficiently high, it could be increased for each succeeding conviction until it was sufficiently high to deter the most indifferent and insolent manager or company.
There, again, is a statement of the views of these men regarding the law. It indicates their intent to observe it, but their opposition to a penalty of imprisonment.
I should like to have it noted that in the action taken by the inspector against these mining companies, the company and the manager in each instance were summonsed, although the present act refers to any mining company, or any company, and does not refer to the manager. I believe my interpretation of section 14 is correct.
I would suggest, therefore, that the hon. member for Champlain ought to bear in mind the debate which took place last year in the senate, and which I read very closely. One senator defending the amendment, who came from a district in which the hon. member's constituency is located, when asked to state the name of some important company or companies which were violating the law, was unable to make reply or to name one company.
I know the hon. member for Champlain has, in certain instances, good grounds for seeking the amendfnent. My contention, however, is that the amendment goes too far, and in terminating my observations I would ask him again seriously to consider the suggestion made, namely to provide for an increased fine rather than a term of imprisonment.

speechtext:
The purpose of this amendment, which I do not for one moment wish to conceal, is to repeal section 106 of the act. I expected that before the bill got into committee I would have had to say a few words, but now that it is in committee I do not think it is necessary to say very much. The section to be repealed reads:
It shall be an illegal practice and an offence against this act for any candidate for election as member to serve in the House of Commons to sign any written document presented to him by way of demand or claim made upon him, by any person-, persons or associations of persons, between the date of the issue of the writ of election and the date of polling, if such document requires such candidate to follow any course of action that will prevent him from exercising freedom of action in parliament if elected, or to resign as such member if called upon to do so by any person, persons or association of persons.

Dominion Elections-Signed Pledges
I believe that this is the first time a section of this kind has been included in our Dominion Elections Act.
For quite a number of years we have been treated to speeches on democracy. We pride ourselves on a democratic Canada; yet in the face of those speeches in favour of democracy and our claims that we want to support democracy we have put into the Dominion Elections Act section 106, which, if it is allowed to remain in the act, in my opinion does away with democracy.
Democracy, as I see it, is the will of the people, and when the people of Canada are refused the right to pledge their candidates I think it is treading the path of dictatorships, which nobody in this house wants for a moment. In the country which I left more than twenty-five years ago demands were made for certain constitutional changes which most hon. members know as Home Rule, and to-day there is Home Rule in that country. Several other demands have been made in other countries; and as the representatives of the people are the only spokesmen that the people have in parliament, if we take away from the people the right to have their candidates sign pledges and to back up the promises they make prior to an election I think we are treading on dangerous ground, ground much more dangerous than perhaps some realize.
I do not think it is necessary for me to say much more. The wording of the section itself as it stand's in the act is sufficient, I think, to prove that it is dangerous, undemocratic, and along the line of dictatorship by parties, particularly those in power.
From the Ottawa Journal of February 23 last, I clipped this item:
Want Preelection Promises Kept
Olympia, Wash., Feb. 23-Political speeches in Washington state may undergo drastic changes if Rep. William J. Pennoek's bill passes. It would Tequire major state officers to add this pledge to their oath:
"I furthermore do promise and swear that to the best of my ability I will endeavour to perform and fulfil all promises made by me during the campaign, as the result of which I was elected to said office."
If we intend to support democracy and keep away from dictatorship, the best thing we can do is get away from section 106 and leave the old act as it stood in that respect.

Mr. Chairman, the difference between my hon. friend (Mr. Fair) and myself lies largely, I think, in what is meant by democracy. I am to some extent responsible for section 106 being in the act, because it was at my suggestion to the committee which

The object of the section is to do away with an abuse, which has grown up in our public life, of a large number of small minority groups endeavouring to hold up a candidate by making him sign pledges with respect to everything under the sun. During the last federal election we were confronted in the district of Quebec with nineteen separate and distinct pledges that we had to sign. As a matter of fact, I will say for the better-class candidates that they did not sign, but the candidates who were not so conscientious about their duties to the public did sign everything that was presented to them. They swallowed them whole. They signed things with which they had no concern whatsoever, such as pledges with respect to real property, with w'hich the dominion parliament has no concern. Certain minority groups have got into the habit of asking everything in order, in some instances, to embarrass the better-class candidates, and in others, to .assist the worst candidates.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter which is before the house at the present time, namely, the ratification of the trade agreement between Canada and the United States, is in my opinion one of the most important subjects which will come before the house during this session. I do not desire to go back very many years into the history of trade agreements between Canada and the United States, but I would remind the house and the country that during the years between 1930 and 1935 there was a great demand in this country, and a growing demand in the United States, for freer trade facilities between these and other lands. So many restrictions and repressions had been put on the exchanging of surplus commodities of the two countries that there was in them both a great diminution in employment, in the standard of living, and in the confidence of the 
producers and the consumers of wealth in these countries, so closely bound together by nature and so well fitted to be in every way the counterpart one of the other in trading matters.
After the last election the people of Canada were much heartened by the speed with which the agreement of 1935 was negotiated between the two governments. When that agreement was signed, within a few weeks of the new administration taking office, it was regarded by the people of Canada generally, regardless of what their party politics were, or the views held in the past about the need and value of trading, as a good omen for the future. That has been abundantly justified by the results which sprang from the signing of that agreement, and the creating of larger opportunities of trade flowing north and south during these years.
The other day one of my hon. friends opposite said that that agreement was not successful ; that it had not worked out as intended because trade in 1938 had receded, compared with what it had been in 1937. As a matter of fact, he was handing great praise to the treaty and to the way in which it had worked out, because, in other words, he was saying that trade in 1937 had increased at a tremendous rate over 1935. The whole world knows that there was a recession in 1938 which affected the United States .particularly and Canada as well. But to-day Canada is coming out of it faster than our neighbours have done; though we have not suffered as badly, nevertheless our trade is bound to be affected by theirs, with or without treaties. That treaty was so successful that by 1937, in less than two years, we had recovered much of the ground lost in employment, in the production of wealth, in trade with the world, and in renewed confidence on the part of the Canadian people in themselves, their land, their institutions and their future.
We in this house know and the government of the day was quite aware of the fact, which has been mentioned by several hon. members, that that treaty was not, as I admit that this new treaty is not, a panacea for all our ills. It would be impossible; it has never been possible in the history of the world for any government to find a single universal remedy for all its troubles. There are groups of men in the country here and there who think they have found a panacea. One group says that all you have to do is to print all the money you want and you will have a solvent for all difficulties, but in their hearts they know better than that.

speechtext:
Well, it is not
usually assumed that we in this house, with all the responsibilities that the electors put upon us, are sent here to discuss other than material problems. It is not assumed generally that we are sent here to discuss particularly the intellectual or the mental or the spiritual problems of the people. There are other forums in which those questions can be debated. We therefore take it for granted that when we speak of problems we refer to the economic and material problems of the country, because the political and social problems have been largely solved in so far as they can be in a place like this.
To continue, the government knew that this theaty of 1935 could not solve, and they are not claiming now that the 1938 treaty can solve, all our problems. It is impossible to deal with the many-sided phases of modem life, and, by virtue of one trading agreement between two countries out of three, remedy all the evils of which we complain. My hon. friend who asked the question knows as well as I do that over large areas of Canada no wealth amounting to anything has been produced in many years. No wealth has been produced in a part of this dominion which formerly produced wealth in great abundance, and consequently he must know that this is one of the things from which we are suffering, and that the trading of surplus wealth from
other areas will not make up for the loss which is entailed by non-production of wealth over so large a part of Canada.
Both the great country to the south of us and ourselves, however, desired a further advancement along the lines now proposed and, as time went on and the value of the agreement was being demonstrated, those who had been opposed to such agreements in Canada and the United States greatly moderated their objections to them, while those who had been in favour of them on general principles now found their arguments backed up by specific reasons, so that there was a willingness to negotiate once more and again to concede more than it had been found practicable to do in the earlier agreement.
"Lo get the most out of such an agreement it was necessary that other countries, if possible, should be negotiated with at ' the same time, and so we found that for the first time in history the three great English-speaking democracies of the northern hemisphere, the United Kingdom, Canada and the United States, by joint efforts, by a spirit of cooperation, by a spirit of compromise here and there on non-essentials if you will, were able to come together and draft treaties mutually satisfactory to them, which it is believed will result in great good in various ways to the three countries participating and to many-other peoples throughout the world.
To the great Secretary of State of the Lmted States much credit is due for the work that he has performed during the last few years in paving the way for these treaties, and I think the people of Canada and of the old land are equally pleased that their governments took a lead in obtaining these results. It was not an easy matter at all because no trading is particularly easy, and the more people you get into the trade the harder it is to bring it to a successful conclusion. Where negotiations had to be carried on between any two of the nations and then referred to the third one, and difficulties removed there, this was bound to necessitate a great deal of work and difficulties could not be avoided. The mutual concessions, however, that had to be made in the articles dealt with in an earlier agreement were finally arranged satisfactorily, and I believe that a great deal of the credit is due to the technical knowledge, the trained skill and the patience exhibited by the officials of this government who had so much to do, in negotiating with their fellow officials of the other countries, with preparing the way for the adoption of these agreements.
1310	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
On the first of January last when the new agreement came into effect we found that eighty per cent of all Canada's external trade was more or less beneficially affected by these treaties. For a country in Canada's position, the fourth greatest exporter of goods in the world, even with a small population of eleven millions, to foe able to negotiate favourable treaties with the two great peoples who purchase from her more than eighty per cent of all of her exports, is something that is well worth rejoicing over, if it is possible to rejoice at all in matters of trade.
A few years ago we heard from time to time-we do not hear it so often to-day- the argument that there is no trade anyhow. People who believe that are naturally not going to be enthusiastic over trade treaties, and I could not blame them for not being enthusiastic over the negotiation of such agreements as this, because if there is no trade in the world, for the reason that every country has too much of everything that there is no way of disposing of anything, which was the classical way in which some of our friends used to express themselves, then there would be no object in negotiating trade treaties at all. But we have never believed that. The economists of the world have never believed it. As a matter of fact, world economists of high mark have never believed at any time that there was being produced in the world a sufficiency of wealth for the needs of those who were producing and would like to consume more of the wealth being turned out by the various industries in the world, primary and secondary.
In 1928 and 1929, when the wheels of industry were running faster and the factories were more fully occupied than ever before, the great Swedish economist, Professor Gustav Cassel, estimated that barely enough wealth was being produced to maintain the peoples of the world on the standard of living that they had been enjoying, and that they wanted not only to maintain but to increase. I do not know of any way by which the standard of living has been raised so much as by trade. It is true that new inventions, skill in handling them and technical education in its proper meaning have contributed to the production of wealth in greater quantity than formerly, but the production of additional wealth in any country is not going to continue unless it can be exchanged, and if it cannot, that industry is going to fall by the wayside. Before I close I am going to allude to one or two developments of that kind in the province from which I come. I think

everyone will agree that if no market is found for the products of those new applications of agricultural industry, the industries wil Icease to expand and to bring wealth to the people affected.
We have sometimes had in this house, from those who are not enthusiastic about this treaty, the argument that trade is a form of war. If that were true, I should not be very much in favour of trade expansion. But I am sure that most people throughout the world to-day are satisfied that trade is not productive of war; neither is it the trading nations who are most inclined to war with one another, nor is the system of private ownership-which is inherent in this treaty- the cause of war. The greatest and best evidence of that is that during all the years in which private ownership and capitalism have flourished in industry and the production and distribution of wealth, in these two great countries lying side by side, probably the most highly capitalized in the world and with the greatest degree of individual freedom and the greatest scope for individual initiative in the world, there has not been the breath of suspicion of war.
I believe that, having succeeded in making these treaties, we should take advantage of them to the utmost possible extent; that we should supply as much wealth as possible to the British and United States markets and should take in exchange as much as possible from those markets in order that we may be paid for what we sell and may enjoy the higher standard of living that such exchanges will make possible. Therefore, even though this debate has continued for a few days, and while most hon. members are ready to vote on it at any time-and I am glad to say that I have found no very strong opposition to the treaty anywhere, and there is no question as to what is going to happen when the vote is taken-I am convinced that the time spent in debating this treaty from various angles that may interest individual members and the people whom they represent is time well spent; for the more a treaty of this kind is discussed and the more familiar our people come to be with its provisions, the more advantage can be obtained from it. I believe that when there has been time for other nations throughout the world to become impressed with the value of this treaty, many of them will also desire to negotiate with these three great English-speaking countries and carry on a wider trade with them and develop freer markets, as we are now doing.

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
In the short time I have, I could not, if I would, go through all the provisions of this agreement, so I am going to limit my argument to the treaty as it affects us as sellers in the United States market. There is, of course, another side that is very important. But if we cannot sell our goods in the United States we shall be less able to pay for the goods we wish to buy in their market, while it is necessary for us to take the goods we buy from them in order to get paid for what we sell to them. And I do not know that one part is more important than the other. But because they fall into two separate classes, and because the concessions that we have made to the United States can be discussed on the budget or on some other occasion, I shall deal with the other side of the question first and look at the concessions that have been made to us in the United States.
With the concessions obtained in 1935 and in 1938 we have had reductions or bindings on 170 items, affecting $124,825,000 worth of sales that we made to them in the year 1937. We also secure the maximum reduction of 50 per cent of the duty on products exported from Canada to the value in 1937 of $56,000,000, or 49 per cent of the total value of dutiable imports from Canada in that year. That alone is sufficient to encourage the sending of more goods to the United States. But for the purpose of my reasoning I am going to deal with some matters that particularly affect either western Canada or the province of Saskatchewan or that part of it which I represent, or some particular industries in Canada that were more in need of assistance than certain other industries. There are many items which I do not intend to touch.
Taking the list of concessions in schedule II, I draw attention to the fact that our metal industries, one great group of our natural industries in this country that has done so much to carry the state through the difficult years through which we have been and are passing, are getting substantial benefit from this agreement. Aluminum, which carried a duty burden of 4 cents a pound going into the United States, has had that duty reduced to 3 cents. On cadmium, the duty, which was 15 cents a pound, is now reduced to 7J cents. Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to be responsible for prolonging this debate more than a few minutes. I do propose, however, to deal with some of the items when the treaty is being considered in committee.
To begin with, in my opinion the whole system employed by [DOT] this government in bringing about these treaties is wrong. I say that because they do not use the system employed in the United States.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) asked the following questions of the ministry on February 15, 1938:
1.	Will the government lay on the table the list of 47 pages of goods on which the United States propose to discuss further reciprocity with Canada as published partly in the local press on January 8, and on which the people of that country were asked to write the Trade Department at Washington to give their views or objections on any of these items with a public hearing on March 14, afforded?
2.	Will the government consider adopting the same method and procedure here in order to give the business men of Canada an opportunity of being heard in the same way by

letter, and a public hearing later, before any proposed agreement is consummated, and not after it?
3. Will the government consider calling into consultation Canadian industrialists and agriculturists regarding the effect of same on the Ottawa agreements, before and not after any agreement or treaty is consummated or proposed ?
In answer to question number two of the hon. member, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated:
The procedure at present adopted by the United States government in connection with current trade agreements - is based upon the fact that agreements concluded under the Trade Agreements Act are not submitted to congress for approval. As the situation in this respect is different in Canada, it is not considered necessary to adopt the United States procedure.
What difference is there? Was this last trade agreement submitted to this parliament before it was signed and before it became law? Were hon. members consulted before this treaty came into effect? This last treaty with the United States came into effect on January 1, 1939; this parliament was called on January 12, and we are now discussing the treaty in the middle of February. In answer to question number three, the Prime Minister stated:
The present practice under which Canadian industrialists, agriculturists, and others interested, may communicate with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or other ministers concerned, on all matters respecting commercial treaty negotiations, is believed to be adequate.
How can Canadian industrialists, agriculturists and others interested approach the government in connection with these matters when they have not the faintest idea of what is being considered by the government? If there ever were a purely political treaty executed by this country, it is the one now before us. It is a treaty in which there is very little thought for the common good. It is a treaty to suit one or two sections of this dominion. Apparently the members from those sections control this government. There are supporters of this government who are to-day hanging their heads in shame. They have not been in this house for the past three weeks, ever since this treaty has been under discussion. They are ashamed of it. My belief is that if the treaty of 1935 had not been put into effect, conditions in this country would have improved to such an extent that there would have been increased employment and increased trade within Canada, and we would have had dominion unity instead of disunity. Our working people would have been happier. The supporters of the government have spent so little time in this debate

Has one of them risen in his place on the floor of this house and defended his position? Not one, Mr. Speaker, not one. I wish to protest against the unfair treatment which has been accorded the market gardeners, the greenhouse industry and the fruit growers of the country by this government in these two treaties. In vegetable growing alone we have a major primary industry. To quote the words of Mr. M. B. Davis and Mr. T. F. Ritchie of the central experimental farm, Ottawa, as delivered at the Carls-Rite hotel, Toronto:
It would seem therefore that we have in this vegetable industry something of real value as a national asset and it is our guess that
[Mr. Lennard.l
the industry is easily worth in its entirety $100,000,000 a year. Such an industry merits attention and deserves support if it is to continue as a source of wealth to this country.
I ask in all seriousness: Has this industry received this consideration? I say, no. The sections of the Canadian fruit and vegetable industry which will suffer most severely under the new arrangements with the United States are the hothouse tomato growers, the pear growers and the asparagus growers. The greenhouse industry is the one branch of market gardening most seriously affected. The hothouse growers of tomatoes find that their overhead is the same to-day as it was several years ago. The cost of coal, labour, et cetera, is at the same level, while the duty has been lowered from 30 per cent in 1935 to a bare 10 per cent at the moment. With the two cents a pound dumping duty removed, these men will be practically forced out of business. They will have to readjust their business, and I do not know what other line of production they can turn to which will permit a profitable use of their hothouses. I know many of them have been scraping along for the past few years. I know of several large plants which cannot afford to close down. They have been running along with small losses in the hope that some government would come along and give them relief so that they might operate successfully in the future. If that does not happen soon, I know many of these concerns will go to the wall. These tomato growers have to compete with a field grown crop, harvested with cheap' labour and receiving a freight subsidy. What chance have they? What protection is 10 per cent against such competition?
While there has been no change in the dumping duty on pears, the Canadian government has agreed to apply the dumping duty for a twelve week period only. This is not sufficient to cover the entire pear season, and the result will be that the threat of United States imports by Canadian canning companies will be a greater menace than ever. In connection with asparagus, the loss is the three per cent excise, five per cent on the general duty and two-fifths of a cent per pound on the dumping duty. When these are all totalled up, it means a material reduction in the protection against United States asparagus, which some canning companies often import for the purpose of smashing Canadian prices when the canning season rolls round.
This afternoon the hon. member for Souris (Mr. McDonald) stated that one-third of the people of Canada were farmers, and that two-thirds of the people of Canada were in-
1316	COMMONS
Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
terested in agriculture. Does he realize that the other one-third he speaks of are in the market gardening and fruit growing industries, which are directly affected by these treaties? If the other third of the population of Canada are in industry, two-thirds of the population of Canada are directly affected by this treaty.
The hon. member for Victoria, Ontario (Mr. McNevin) stated some time ago that he thought the new trade agreements would help the woollen and knit goods industry. I wonder if he really thinks that, or if he has given it any thought at all. I should like to give a few facts in connection with the woollen and knit goods industry.
1.	The industry is essentially Canadian with eighty-five per cent of its $92,000,000 investment being supplied by Canadian investors.
2.	Ninety-eight per cent of the goods made by these mills must be sold within Canada.
This is because Canadian wage scales are higher than in other countries, or because the textile tariffs of other countries are against Canadian textiles. Therefore our industry is dependent upon its Canadian market.
3.	The government in again lowering the tariff in our Canadian market will give workers in other countries added production and Canadian workers less.
In 1937 our textile industry bought from Australia, direct, over $2,000,000 worth of wool, which constitutes twenty-four per cent of Canada's purchases from that country. It bought from New Zealand over $3,000,000 of wool, which constitutes fifty-eight per cent of the total imports from that country.
In addition to Australian and New Zealand products the industry purchased approximately double the above quantities through Bradford, England, in the form of raw and partly processed wool.
These purchases by Canada from empire countries were a substantial consideration in negotiating trade treaties with these countries, from which Canadian workers in other industries benefit.
Thus, the woollen and knit goods industry contributes in a major way to empire trade, both in its actual purchases from empire countries, and in tariff concessions to competitive empire products, in return for empire trade concessions to Canadian natural and farm products.
The widespread and comprehensive nature of the industry is clearly demonstrated by the fact that its $25,000,000 direct wages are paid into eighty-two municipalities in Ontario; thirty-nine municipalities in Quebec; eighteen municipalities in the maritimes, and seven municipalities in western Canada.

The present economic condition of the textile industry in the United States is forcing her to seek openings in Canada for the surplus production she is not internally absorbing. Further concessions in tariff would merely aggravate the danger to our Canadian industry. This condition illustrates the seriousness of a tariff reduction to a country having such economic difficulties as the United States portrays.
It is of the utmost concern to the woollen and knit goods industry that because of the favoured nation treaties which Canada now has with twenty-two foreign countries, any tariff concessions which are given to the United States must automatically be given to all these others. Unfortunately these others include Japan, Italy, Germany and Czechoslovakia, all of which are textile producing countries operating on wage scales ridiculously low compared with those prevailing in Canada. It would be disastrous to this Canadian industry if the products of that class of foreign production were given an opportunity to gain any further foothold in our Canadian market.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the workmen of this country have been sold out to foreign capital; their very jobs have been jeopardized by these two treaties.
In addition to the confusion and in many cases chaos that has been created in industry through these treaties, there is the additional paralyzing effect of the uncertainty surrounding the excise tax. We read in the press that it will possibly be removed altogether. But who knows? Consequently the industry of this country is to an extent at a standstill, awaiting the outcome. To put it squarely to this government, they are shirking their duty in withholding this information, and it will jeopardize the very existence of many industries, especially in eastern Canada, if this question is not settled very soon. I say that, Mr. Speaker, in all seriousness. I have been approached by industrialists during the past two or three weeks, and they say: "This treaty is signed, and I suppose we shall have to make the best of it, but what is the government going to do about the excise tax? With the present uncertainty our business is paralyzed; we do not want to buy, and people will not buy from us because we do not know, and they do not know, what is going to be done about the three per cent excise tax." It is one of the most serious stumbling blocks before industry in this country at this moment, and this government should end the uncertainty at the earliest possible moment.

This trade treaty is much broader than any we have had before. It includes the British Empire. I cannot understand the opposition voting against a trade treaty with the British empire. For years they used to come into the house, wrap themselves in the union jack and talk about patriotism, waving the flag in our faces. For over thirty years I have heard a great deal about the flag in Toronto, and now that we have a trade treaty with Great Britain; now that

The leader of the opposition says that he cannot vote for the treaty. He opposes it for several reasons. First, he says that it means greater competition in industry. Well, I am sure that the people who sent me here will thank heaven for that. They are paying far too much for their farm implements and there is need for some competition to bring about a reduction in the prices of those articles which they have to buy. This will be a blessing to them.
Next he says that this is the beginning of the destruction of the British preference. Well, now! Imagine the Conservative party starting to nurse the British preference! Why, that was the child of the Liberal party. The Conservative party tried hard to kill it at its birth; yet now they say it is not safe in the hands of its parents. Adjustments are made in the British preference, but it is not destroyed, and I think it will be many a day before it is destroyed-perhaps never.
Next he says that he opposes the treaty because it injures our Canadian traffic, the traffic north and south. That is an old Tory fallacy. Liberalism, let me point out, always tries to bring the producer and the consumer as close together as possible, but the Conservative policy for the last thirty years has been to put up toll gates and barriers between the two. They are constantly doing it. Dear knows, nature has provided enough barriers between producer and consumer without our adding extra ones. Time is a barrier, and a deflater between producer and consumer. Weather is a deflater, because commodities may suffer in going through tropical or cold climates as the case may be. Transportation, freight rates, a hill on the highway-anything that helps to keep traffic back is a deflater and destroyer of trade and commerce.
But the Conservative party are not satisfied with that. They want to put more obstructions in the way, and they complain that this treaty injures our Canadian traffic, the trade going north and south. I suggest to the leader of the opposition and those who approve his policy that he get a highway which is not too congested, one that goes round in a circle, and travel over it for so many miles before depositing cargo. Perhaps they would then vote for the treaty.
The next point he complains about is the removal of the excise tax. The removal of the tax, it is said, will have a paralyzing effect. Its removal will not paralyze the people of my constituency, and the sooner it
tMr. Blair.]
goes the better. In fact, in my opinion, it should never have been imposed.
I always enjoy listening to the Conservatives heckling a bit once in a while, because it gives me an idea of what brand of politics they have. The last time I spoke in this house I was accused in the house in Toronto of denouncing the Conservatives. No. I do not denounce the Conservatives; it is the Tories I denounce. There is a difference between Tory and Conservative. The Tory votes by tradition. He goes to church once a year, some time about July.

speechtext:
We need trade, because it is impossible for a country like Canada with her large surplus of raw materials to live without exporting.
We are charged frequently with not cooperating. Let me say that the King government has cooperated fully with Neville Chamberlain in all his actions during the recent critical conditions in Europe. They also did so at the time when the change in the sovereign took place. These matters are very important. Naturally when a Liberal government in Canada cooperates fully with a Conservative government in Great Britain we receive some criticism, we expect that. But we have no apologies to make. We believe Neville Chamberlain will go down in history as the greatest British statesman in many years, and I believe that the name of Mackenzie King will be associated with his for his splendid cooperation.
This treaty may seem to be merely an economic one, but it is of much more far-reaching importance than merely an economic asset. I have here an extract from a speech of a certain man, I do not know how true it is to his inmost mind because I read his speeches in the Hastings by-election; I have them on file, and whenever I look at them they fairly make me sick. But he has been reading passages from some author and he made this declaration at Fort William, as reported in the St. Catharines Standard of January 28, 1939:
. . . Colonel George Drew went on to assert that "The one hope of the world is a complete understanding between the British empire and the United States to work together in the preservation of peace, a movement in which we Canadians are the interpreters, the ambassadors between the empire and the United States." Which, most people will agree, we think, sums up Canada's position to a nicety.
There is a passage of which I do not think Colonel Drew was the author, but I give him credit for saying it at a public gathering. It means more than most might think. It is the soul of old Joseph Chamberlain; it may have come from some of his writings. Joseph Chamberlain believed in the unification of the British people the world over. He was narrow in his racial ideas, but was ambitious for the unification of the British people. It also expresses the soul and spirit of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who sought for cooperation with and unification of the British people by means of the British preference and reciprocity, something similar to what we are having now. It was the spirit of J. A. Macdonald, editor of the Globe, who preached the unification of the British people, throughout the United States. Now we have Colonel Drew, and if ever a man had a chance to do a little missionary work, if Colonel Drew would spread that doctrine through the club rooms in Toronto, it would be a godsend for some of the Toronto organizations. That spirit is strongly opposed to some of the ideas we hear in this house. If Colonel Drew puts forward that idea in the Ontario house he will not meet with any opposition, because the keynote and foundation of Liberalism is freer trade and better understanding among the nations of the world.
There is one point I might mention in closing; it is in the spirit of Neville Chamberlain that if a nation is so confined that it has not sufficient territory to support its people, that nation should be allowed to get more territory where there are vacant lands, because people are not going to be content to starve on territory on which it is impossible for them to live. There are nations in the world which are in that position; I believe Neville Chamberlain is anxious to give them relief, and I have great faith that he will do it, although he is being bitterly opposed by many British people. But every nation has a right to live and obtain food and clothing, and if they do not have it at home I think some latitude should be given to them to enable them to secure it in other parts of the world.
The great cause of world peace lies behind this treaty. I know there are hon. members opposite who do not think that; they think this treaty is merely an economic problem. Of course it is that, and a vast one; but its object is also the tying together of the English speaking peoples which will be a factor in our national protection. It tends toward making an economic unit of the British people, and I believe that with that protection we shall be relieved of having to spend as much money for defence as we

otherwise would have to spend. I think there will be found a great degree of unification among the British peoples, and it is even broader and wider than that. While Great Britain asks all the dominions to come in, they are extending the glad hand to all nations possessing the spirit of British democracy to come hither and join with them in this great union. That means much. The treaty now before us is all right as far as it goes, but the matter does not end there. Great Britain extends the glad hand to all the democracies of the world. This is the first great step toward the unification of all the democracies and all the British peoples
It was with a great deal of regret that I saw the leader of the opposition rise in his place and tell us why he would not vote for this treaty. These men in the far comer rise in their places and talk against the treaty, but we do not know which way they are going. I have faith in the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party; I generally know which way he will vote, and I have never found him opposing a properly negotiated trade treaty which would bring about lower duties. I have not faith in all hon. members in that comer, but I have faith in him. I think some of these men are talking one way, while they would like to talk the other way. I believe the Conservatives talk one way, while they would like to vote the other way. I believe the leader of the opposition would like to vote for this treaty; yet he is speaking against it.

They remind me of a story, which I should not tell, of two English cockneys in a London fog who were going round a comer rather quickly. One fellow was cock-eyed and the other was cross-eyed. Then ran into each other, and one fellow said, "Why can't you look where you're going?" to which the other replied, "Why can't you go where you're looking?" Hon. members should look where they are going and go where they are looking. If you talk against this treaty, be men enough to vote against it. If you have faith in this treaty, quit talking against it and approve it. I suggest to those from western Canada that it would be a great mistake to vote against this treaty, which means much to the farmers of both the east and the west. It may not mean much to industry, but it is a great benefit to the dominion as a whole.
