Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay this house for more than a few minutes, but I have a couple of points in mind that I do not think have been touched upon. In the six weeks I have been in this house listening to the debates I have become convinced of at least one thing, and it is that any and every government is condemned. It is ridiculed if it does nothing and seriously maligned if it attempts to do anything. I believe the government considered every aspect of this trade agreement and took the advice of competent men before presenting this measure to parliament. I am sure their opinion has not been changed by the debate that has taken place; on the contrary, I think a great many arguments have been presented that would tend to increase their faith in the agreement.
There is one argument I should like to present, and I do not intend to bring forth the scrap-book in order to prove it. Most of the quotations that have been read in this house during the past five or six weeks, particularly during the debate on the trade agreement, have not proved anything but the colour of the politics of those who wrote the articles. I believe this is a good treaty, and I will try to illustrate one of my reasons for so believing by citing the exports of milk and cream. The milk quota that Canada is allowed to send to the United States is 3,000,000 gallons, while the cream quota has been set at 1,500,000 gallons. The two together, converted into gallons of milk, mean 18,000,000 gallons which, if converted into butter, would mean 9.000,000 pounds. If we could remove 9,000.000 pounds of the surplus butter that is in Canada today, there would be quite a different picture in the market price of the remainder.
I mention that one point because it holds true in regard to any other commodity that might be suggested. The 1,000,000 bushels of potatoes is, in itself, not a great quantity, but surely it is not anticipated that the whole province of New Brunswick or the whole province of British Columbia will go into the growing of potatoes. In my opinion it is fortunate for us that we have to the south a country of 130,000,000 people where we can sell our small surplus, thereby keeping our own markets firm, without seriously interfering with their markets. If we should attempt to increase our quotas beyond what may be sufficient to take care of our surpluses, I think we would be on dangerous ground which might bring about the cancellation of the agreement.
There is one other point I should like to make in connection with lumber, in which we in British Columbia are very much interested.

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
Is it fair that the lumber of British Columbia should be sold in any market which does not return a fair, reasonable profit? By that I mean a profit which will give the labourers fair wages, which will provide a fair return on the money invested and which will allow some profit to those doing the business. In the old country we have to compete against cheap European labour, and on the lumber we ship there we cannot make sufficient profit to make it worth while. I say it is not fair that the natural resources of this country should be wasted. It takes a hundred years to grow a tree. Why should that tree be cut down with no one profiting from it?
It has been stated several times that United States business men were too smart for our business men. Well, I should not like to say that in many of the club rooms throughout this country unless there was a handy means of exit. I will say this: I believe the United States business man is shrewd. He is just so shrewd in making a deal that he would not use that shrewdness in a deal of this kind, because he wants it to last. If you want to trade in sharp practice you had better get into the horse trading business, not into permanent business conditions. I think the United States business man is just smart enough to try to make a good deal, yet one that is going to be fair and lasting to us all.
My last word is this: This is not a cure-all for all the ills we have in Canada. It is something that will help. Not only will it help, but it will help considerably. I hope the government, before parliament prorogues, will have many other measures brought forward which will assist in solving our problems.
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln): Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with just a few of the brief comments I desire to make on the trade agreement which is now being so fully discussed in the house, I want to crave your indulgence by permitting me to speak from the seat properly belonging to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Marsh). My understanding is that hon. members are supposed to address the house from the seats allocated to them, but unfortunately those of us in the back row are still within the shadows, and I would appreciate making my remarks from a seat which is not my own.
First, may I say a word to the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) in reply to his reference respecting goods we sell in the United States, and the concessions made to us. He referred to the circumstance of 225,000 cattle being permitted to be sold in the United States. I happen to have before me 71492-84 i
the trade agreement, and I have been trying to find the joker in the pack. The reason why Mexico grabbed off nearly 50 per cent of the quota for the first three months is found at the bottom of the page, where it is stated that some consultations might be held before the quotas are finally established. That is the stipulation in the further provision set out in the foot note. I can now realize why Mexico captured nearly 50 per cent of the quota.
When I was home a week ago I learned about one cattle raiser who had fattened about forty head of cattle which he anticipated selling in Buffalo. It was his intention to make an effort to sell in the Buffalo market to which reference was made a few moments ago. He made inquiries, and the reply was, " Well, the only chance you have to take advantage of the lower rate of duty is to wait until after April 1, then watch your step and get in ahead of Mexico."
I have listened attentively to the many speeches which have been made on the merits and demerits of the Canada-United States and Great Britain-United States trade agreements. It is not my desire to prolong the debate, but in looking at yesterday's Hansard I find that at adjournment last night the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred particularly to the fact that in all probability we would continue this debate through the entire day. Therefore I assume any hon. member has a right to continue the debate and make his observations.
At the outset I want to tell the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) that it would not be in the mind of any right thinking Canadian to think of anything else than trading with other countries in a legitimate way. I believe Canada has demonstrated that by her example in the past, no matter what government might be in power. Canada is endowed with a great wealth of natural resources. No one will dispute that our future prosperity is, in a large measure, dependent upon the legitimate development of those resources. I am one who believes that far too much of our raw materials is now being shipped out of Canada without giving our Canadian workmen a greater share of the employment which would result from a greater development of our resources at home.
Many countries are not as richly blessed as we are, and were we more fully to protect our Canadian workmen by seeing to it that they enjoy a fuller measure of their reward, I believe that at least part of our unemployment problem would be solved. Surely there is no one who will argue that countries needing
1322	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
our products would refuse to buy from us if we took steps more adequately to protect our own workmen.
It is interesting to note that predictions made from this side of the house early in the debate are showing evidence of coming true. I believe it was the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) and some other hon. members from this side who drew to the attention of the government the fact that the three per cent reduction in excise tax on items covered in the trade agreements Would ultimately be extended in a general way, and that in reality this amounts to a further three per cent reduction in duty.
I believe recent observations of ministers of the government would indicate that this result is almost inevitable. It has been mentioned by one minister that this will probably mean a loss of several million dollars. I believe it was not many days ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) indicated that this possible loss of revenue resulting from the decreased excise tax would be offset by increased trade. Let me say a word about that increased trade which would be required to make up the loss in revenue, which would probably amount to several millions of dollars.
I have endeavoured to ascertain what percentage of our imports are of manufactured products and what percentage are the products of basic industries. The best information I have received makes one hesitate to quote figures, because they are at variance, depending on the basis of calculations. I have no hesitation, however, in making the definite statement that a very large percentage of our imports is of manufactured products. Accordingly, if we are to increase our trade with countries which demand that we accept their manufactured products, how will that affect the jobs of our Canadian workmen? I say that in many instances they will be sacrificed to countries where the standard of living is much lower than we hope to maintain among our Canadian workers.
I should like to deal a little more at length with fruit and vegetables, because that is one item which is of vital importance to the peninsula from which I come. We see vast quantities of fruits and vegetables coming in from the United States. Figures have been placed on Hansard in answer to questions asked of the government, and it is not necessary to attempt to prove this statement at this time. The fact is that vast amounts of fruits and vegetables are being imported

from the United States. Why do we find the fruit and vegetable growers of Canada during the past few months urging upon the government the great necessity of giving further protection to this great primary industry? If they were not alarmed, would they have gathered funds, as they did from their depleted revenues, to send three or four representatives to Washington to make a final fight for their rights? My information is that in one part of Canada where the growers were vitally affected, they raised the sum of $2,500 to send a few of their qualified men to plead their case in Washington. One has only to read the resolutions which have emanated from recent meetings of fruit and vegetable growers to realize how serious they consider their position to be. My opinion is that any government that was alive to the needs of the fruit and vegetable growers of this country would have worked in closer harmony instead of requiring these men to take these drastic steps to protect their interests.
It is not my desire to indulge in repetitions, and I urge hon. members to study the tables which were placed on Hansard last evening, I believe by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber). I am in possession of a much more extensive survey than that which was placed on Hansard by the hon. member, and which appears on page 1259. I could add many more items to those already in print which would indicate the same trend of reduced protection and shortened in-season periods with which the fruit and vegetable growers are faced.
The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) referred to the concessions which had been made to us. I should like to place on Hansard some of the concessions which have been made to the United States. I have in my hand a bulletin prepared by the American Institute of Food Distribution, and I should like to place on Hansard a few excerpts from this booklet which is dated November 19, two days after the treaty was signed. I call particular attention to the heading of this article, which reads:
This digest of the agreement between the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom, including some fifty colonies, was prepared by the food institute staff from official materia] furnished by Washington.
This document was prepared from official material furnished by Washington. I quote:
Two new reciprocal trade agreements negotiated by Mr. Hull with the United Kingdom and her colonies and Canada-his 19th and 20th-cover the largest trading countries in the world. It applies to all parts of the British empire, including more than fifty non-selfgoverning colonies, with the exception of Australia, New Zealand, Union of South Africa,

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
Ireland, India, Burma and South Rhodesia. It goes into effect January 1 for an initial period of three years.
American farm products on which Great Britain granted concessions were valued in 1936 at more than $200,000,000. Our imports on which concessions were granted amounted to $141,500,000 in 1937. Canada has lowered duties on American products which in 1937 were valued at $241,000,000. American concessions to Canada covered products whose trade in 1937 totalled $121,000,000.
As far as it relates to the food industry, we got the best of the negotiations with Great Britain. We gave only negligible concessions on food in return for the major concessions Great Britain granted. Our principal concessions consisted of duty reductions in manufactured articles.
In the Canadian agreement, duties which were reduced in 1936 were further reduced. We gained substantial concessions on fresh, canned and dried fruits and vegetables in return for concessions on lumber, meats, fishery products, dairy products and some minor items like frozen blueberries. Following are analyses of individual bargains struck with Great Britain and Canada:
I want to repeat that this article is based on information supplied to this institute by Washington. The first item we hear about is the six cent preference on wheat. They say:
Wheat-Duty free treatment instead of six cents per bushel should prove of marked value -duty of this size often sufficient to divert trade. Concession should also benefit transportation business because, of transshipments. United Kingdom is leading wheat import market of the world. Formerly one-fourth of United States exports went there. In 1930 shipments were 39,267,000 bushels, 20-1 per cent of United Kingdom's wheat imports; dropped to 9,000 bushels, -05 per cent of the total, in 1933. In 1937 United States supplied 6,485,000 bushels, 3-6 per cent. United States probably will continue now on an export basis.
Then we come to oatmeal, rolled and flake oats, in connection with which they say:
Reduction of one-third should help restore substantial part of the former American share of United Kingdom market, which ranged from eleven to twenty-eight per cent from 1927 to 1931. New British duty in 1932 forced imports to decline heavily and since 1934 they have virtually ceased.
I come now to lard. Somebody has said that the farmers in some parts of this country are smiling. But what has been done about lard?
Lard-10 per cent ad valorem duty removed. This is the third ranking agricultural item in value imported by the United Kingdom (after cotton and tobacco) with the United States sending 55 per cent of its exports to the United Kingdom in 1937 compared with 29 per cent in 1929. Our lard business increased steadily until around 1934 (92 per cent) but from then on the American share dropped to around 38 per cent. Duty removal will tend to check the trend toward substitution of other fats and oils, also enable American lard to make substantial quantitative gains in United Kingdom.
I come next to apples, and a great many members of this house know something about apples:
Apples, fresh-reduced duty equivalent to 16 per cent ad valorem compared with 24 per cent, should help America regain a substantial portion of the market displaced by former duty. United States encouraging cooperation of apple exporters with empire fruits council to secure orderly marketing in United Kingdom, long the most important outlet for American apples, taking about 40 per cent of our exports-which comprise 10 per cent of our total crop.
There are many other items which time will not permit me to mention, but there are one or two more points in particular to which I wish to refer. The article goes on to refer to United States concessions to the United Kingdom, and then to concessions obtained from Canada by the United States. It says:
Concessions obtained from Canada (by United States)
Trade advantages are extended to many major farm products of the United States, including fruits and vegetables, meat products, grains and grain products. Agreement covers agricultural products valued at $47,000,000 in 1937, representing 90 per cent of all Canadian imports ot our farm products.
Those are the concessions obtained from Canada, according to this report. It goes on:
Fresh fruits and vegetables constitute the chief item in the concessions granted by Canada.
There are other items, Mr. Speaker, which time will not permit me to mention.
Is it any wonder, that the fruit and vegetable growers have recently urged upon the government the necessity of 100 per cent fruit content in all processed fruits exported to the United Kingdom? I know that this question is giving the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) serious concern, and that he is giving it fair consideration. He must recognize that it is one of the last hopes our fruit and vegetable growers have left, and I strongly urge the government to listen to this plea of our growers.
Surely if this government, when negotiating these trade agreements, had taken our many Canadian interests more into their confidence, our primary and secondary producers would have been better served.
I do urge upon this government, and upon the new government that I anticipate will be formed in the very near future after the next election, and not by the party opposite, that they take steps to supply the fruit and vegetable industry with more accurate statistics. Acreages and values now supplied are wholly misleading and incorrect, and the growers have been complaining of that for years. Surely the industry deserves more consideration in that respect.
1324	COMMONS
Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
And dove-tailed in with all this is the effect which the treaty is going to have on employment. Primary and secondary industry supplies the employment for our people, and the curtailment of industry has an immediate effect on employment. I know this question is giving the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) great concern, and he has probably only scratched the surface of the situation. But still we find headlines like this relating even to the city of Ottawa: "More unemployed men of Ottawa at Union Mission than ever before." So you do not have to go outside Ottawa to realize what the unemployment situation is. That headline appeared in this morning's Ottawa Journal. The day before yesterday eight young men appeared before the magistrate in my own city-eight in one day-all under twenty years of age. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this inroad on the basic and secondary industries of this country is the main factor in the unemployment situation.
We hear some members of the house praising this government because, they say, the consumer is able to buy this or that article a cent or two cheaper, although it is because we are increasing our purchases from countries where labour can be bought for a song. But who heard the consumer complaining a few years ago about the cent or two extra they had to pay for what they bought when everybody in the country was receiving a pay envelope? The conclusion is obvious. We must protect our basic and secondary industries against the inroads of cheap competition, and then our unemployment problems will immediately begin to disappear.
I note that the hon. Minister of Labour, speaking in Toronto this week, suggested that reductions be made in provincial governments. I suggest that he begin at Ottawa to find the solution for a balanced budget. Every taxpayer in this country is awaiting with anxiety the budget soon to be brought down by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). We have had an expression of opinion in the last few days from a small cross-section of one part of Canada, in the ballots that have been sent to every member of this house. Surely it is time that this government and all governments woke up to the lavish expenditures by governments and to our increasing national debt. If it continues, I warn the minister that the recent flood of ballots into Ottawa from one small cross-section of the country will be insignificant compared with the outcry that will be raised against this government from coast to coast if the next budget presents no evidence of economy being practised. I think it behooves this govern-

ment not to talk about provincial governments first cutting down their expenditures and balancing their budgets. It is all very well to talk about reductions by the provinces but Canada is looking to Ottawa to lead the way.
I have just one other thought in closing. We have heard considerable in this debate about economic appeasement, but there is an appeasement required within the boundaries of Canada that is far more necessary at this moment than to attempt, as has been done in this house, to raise the cry of international appeasement from without. We have all heard in our school days the tale of Nero fiddling while Rome burned, but I see from press reports to-night that there is further provincial appeasement confronting this government and of a nature that will keep them busy during the next few months to come.
I am in full accord with the principle of trading with nations that desire to trade with us on a reasonable basis, but I am definitely opposed to trade agreements that take away a part of the birthright of our Canadian people.
